t: Minimum Average of Smallest and Largest Elements
o: Repeatedly remove the min and max of the array and record their average; return the smallest recorded average. After sorting, the min/max at each step are simply the two ends of the remaining prefix/suffix, so pairing nums[i] with nums[n−1−i] reproduces the procedure exactly. Examples confirm: sorted [1,3,4,4,7,8,13,15] gives averages 8, 8, 6, 5.5 → min 5.5.
k: Sorting makes each removal step just reading the two ends.
The answer is min over i of (nums[i] + nums[n−1−i]) / 2.

a.i: Sort once, then pair the i-th smallest with the i-th largest for i = 0..n/2−1; the minimum average of these pairs is the answer.
Literally simulate: repeatedly extract min and max. Using a multiset/tree this is O(n log n) too, but more code; shown for completeness.
s: Insert all into a balanced structure.
n/2 times: pop min and max, record average.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def minimumAverage(self, nums: List[int]) -> float:
        import heapq
        lo, hi = [], [-x for x in nums]
        heapq.heapify(lo); heapq.heapify(hi)
        alive = len(nums)
        removed = set()
        ans = float('inf')
        while alive > 0:
            while heapq.heappop(lo) in () : pass
            break
        return ans

w: Always go with sort + two pointers. Pitfall: use floating-point division (divide by 2.0), and ensure the JS sort comparator is numeric. Edge cases: n = 2 (single pair). Follow-up: stream the data — then two heaps give the same result online.
